extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, logicians, mathematicians and researchers in mathematical reasoning/automated theorem proving
extracted.subtask_description: Developing a conceptual account of what a 'plan' for a mathematical proof is by analysing the planning agency of the agent(s) who carry out proof activities; connects Bratman's planning theory to proof practice and to modular presentation of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof activity vs. written proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof (as a written/static object) is a sequence of deductive steps, while the corresponding proof activity is a sequence of deductive inferences (epistemic actions); the written proof is a report of the proof activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction when analyzing or producing proofs: the written text often omits the search/trial-and-error stages of the proof activity. Figure 1 illustrates the isomorphism. Evaluate whether the written proof adequately reports the sequence of inferences an intended agent would need to carry out to acquire the theorem (audience-relative requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan attributed to the agent (not the proof object)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of a mathematical proof is conceived as the plan of the agent(s) who carried out the corresponding proof activity — i.e., plans are ascribed to the planner, not merely to the static proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish human-planned proofs from proofs found by random search or brute-force computation (we are more willing to attribute a plan to the mathematician's activity than to a computer's random discovery). This affects how one judges authorship, explanation, and understanding. Compare to alternative accounts (e.g., Bundy) that attribute plans to proofs themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan as an ordered tree of proving intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan for a proof activity is an ordered tree whose nodes are proving intentions, the root is the proving intention corresponding to the theorem, and where each ordered set of children is a subplan obtained via practical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating a proof, represent its plan as a hierarchical tree (see Figure 5 and Appendix). Check that each parent→children relation corresponds to an instance of practical reasoning and that execution of the tree yields the sequence of deductive inferences reported in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving intentions: 'to show' and 'to infer' (atomic plan elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic kinds of proving intentions are identified: 'To show C from [P1,...,Pn]' (proving intentions of type 'to show') and 'To infer C from [P1,...,Pn]' (proving intentions of type 'to infer'). These are the atoms/nodes of plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate linguistic markers in texts (proving verbs like 'we show that', 'we must show that', 'we infer that') and map them to the corresponding schema notation (Pi ⇒ C). Use these to build the plan-tree; 'to infer' intentions typically correspond to executable deductive inferences (actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentions are plan-states: partial, hierarchical, and commitment-bearing (Bratman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on Bratman: intentions are embedded in plans, are often only partially specified at a time, have hierarchical structure (intentions can contain more specific intentions) and involve commitment that coordinates future reasoning and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs/presentations for evidence of such commitments and hierarchical structure. Recognize partial specification as normal (not a flaw) but requiring mechanisms (practical reasoning) to fill in details later. Example analogy: planning a trip to Hawaii (partial intentions about dates/transport).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reasoning: mechanism that fills in plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reasoning is the process by which an agent transforms a given proving intention into one or several more specific proving intentions arranged in a subplan. It is the central step-by-step process by which plans are constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing a proof, identify instances where a higher-level 'to show' intention is expanded into sub-intentions (e.g., 'show A=B' → 'show A⊆B' and 'show B⊆A'). Fraleigh's proof is used as an explicit example of such transformations. Check that each parent→children transformation is plausible/principled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical methods as rule-like schemas transforming intentions into subplans
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical method is a rule (schema) that transforms an input proving intention into one or several output proving intentions (a subplan), e.g. 'To show A=B: 1. Show A⊆B; 2. Show B⊆A; 3. Infer A=B'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and make explicit the method-schema(s) used in constructing subplans; this improves communicability. Consider order-of-execution constraints, implicit inferential steps, and when the method yields deterministic subplans versus commutative/ordering-insensitive steps (represent via equivalence classes if needed). Examples: 'replace by definition' and 'set equality via mutual subset' schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity in proof presentation (modular presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans can be presented modularly by encapsulating subplans (modules) so that details are hidden or expanded depending on the chosen modular description; modularity supports comprehensibility, communicability, readability, and rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing proofs, choose module boundaries to suit the intended audience: encapsulate low-level inferential detail into modules and present a higher-level tree/blueprint. Evaluate modular presentations by whether modules correctly encapsulate practical reasoning and whether they preserve the ability to reconstruct omitted details when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as grasping the plan (structure + practical reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a mathematical proof is characterized as grasping its underlying plan: (1) grasping the ordered-tree structure (how proving intentions fit into the tree), and (2) grasping the practical reasoning behind each parent→children connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of explanatory power or understanding should check both components. A presentation that shows only low-level steps without revealing the hierarchical plan may fail to provide understanding; conversely, a mere outline without showing how sub-intentions are generated can also fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-relativity and implicit hypotheses/premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses of proving intentions and premises of deductive steps are often left implicit in texts; the agent must belong to the intended audience (i.e., be able to carry out the corresponding inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing proofs, make explicit appropriate definitions and hypotheses for the intended audience; when evaluating, consider whether omitted premises are reasonable for the stated audience. Anti-pattern: excessive implicitness that prevents the intended audience from performing required inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partiality and flexibility of plans (Pólya's guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans should not be rigidly fixed prematurely; problem-solvers keep plans 'fluid' and flexible to adapt to unforeseen difficulties and exploit productive failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating proof discovery or in pedagogical contexts, value designs that leave space for revision and adaptation. For automated or formalized presentations, preserve a notion of flexible subplans or allow plan revision operators to mirror human problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution vs. discovery: search, dead-ends, and reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of discovering a proof typically involves search, trial-and-error, and dead-ends; the written proof reports only the successful sequence, omitting many search steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of epistemology, pedagogy, or designing theorem-proving tools, distinguish between (a) the discovery process (planning + search) and (b) the polished report. When producing documentation or tools, consider capturing salient failed attempts or heuristics that contributed to discovery if they are epistemically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit representation of deductive steps and implicit inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Making explicit the deductive steps (including those left implicit by authors) and the corresponding 'to infer' intentions clarifies how the plan executes into a sequence of inferences (example: Fitch-style rendering of Fraleigh's proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating clarity and rigor of a proof, check whether implicit inferential steps that are essential to the plan are recoverable or should be made explicit. Use explicit representations (Fitch-style, labelled inferences, Ii notation) to map proving intentions to concrete inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing human planning account from automated proof-planning frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-centered planning (Bratman-style) attributes plans to agents and emphasizes intentions and practical reasoning, whereas proof-planning frameworks in ATP (Bundy et al.) often treat plans as structures attached to proofs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing automated theorem-proving or interactive proof systems aimed at human-style output, choose frameworks that preserve agentive notions (intentions, partial plans, modularity) if the goal is human comprehensibility; be explicit about where the system's approach diverges from human planning.
